title: Amir Khusrau Sings Hind and Iran

title_i18n.en: Amir Khusrau Sings Hind and Iran

subtitle: The poet of sultans whose songs follow the saints
region: Patiyali, Delhi, Multan, Bengal and Nizamuddin
moral: A bridge of words can outlive empires.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh, Qiran-us-Sadain, Nuh Sipihr and Tughlaq Nama
sources.note: Surviving works that make Khusrau both poet and historical witness.
Conversations of Nizamuddin Auliya with references to the Chishti circle.

sources.citation: Sunil Sharma, Amir Khusraw: The Poet of Sultans and Sufis (Oneworld, 2005)
sources.note: Key modern English biography and literary guide.

dialogue.text: In the age of the Delhi Sultans, Amir Khusrau of Hind and Iran sings for courts and khanqahs, weaving India and Persia into one unending song.
Born in 1253 at Patiyali to a Turk father and an Indian mother, Khusrau grows up between two tongues, hearing Persian inside the house and Hindavi in the lanes.

panels.shot: wide shot of caravan entering city

dialogue.text: Delhi, crowded and restless under the early Sultanate, draws the young poet. Behind its stone walls, soldiers drill, clerks count, and men of letters seek patrons.
Khusrau finds his place among Delhi’s poets, shaping Persian verses for gatherings that move between praise and wit, prayer and politics.
As Balban’s stern rule hardens Delhi, Khusrau’s pen enters the courtly world. He learns how poets serve power, and how words record both favor and fear.

panels.shot: dynamic wide shot over battlefield plain

dialogue.text: Under different sultans he travels with campaigns to places like Multan and Bengal, seeing conquest up close and turning war’s thunder into measured Persian masnavis.

panels.shot: tabletop close-up with manuscript and hand

dialogue.text: In works like Khazain-ul-Futuh, he praises the Delhi Sultans, yet also leaves a record of forts taken, roads built, mosques raised, and the city’s uneasy grandeur.
He serves eight sultans, but his heart leans toward one saint. In Delhi, the road from palace to Nizamuddin Auliya’s humble dwelling becomes Khusrau’s true path.
Amir Hasan Sijzi’s Fawaid-ul-Fuad preserves the saint’s words and the circle around him. Khusrau is part of this listening world, where poetry bows before inner truth.
For Khusrau, sound itself becomes devotion. Later qawwali circles remember him as master of sung praise, even as scholars carefully trace which melodies truly go back to his time.

panels.shot: street-level wide shot in Delhi bazaar

dialogue.text: He writes masnavis and histories in Persian, yet his ear loves Hindavi. In riddles and songs of the street, he catches the everyday music of north India.

dialogue.speaker: amir_khusrau
dialogue.text: This tongue of Hind is sweet on the lips, sharp in the heart.
In Nuh Sipihr, he praises India with detail and pride, describing its people, crafts, and learning. He speaks of Hind not as borderland, but as a world in itself.
From Qiran-us-Sadain to Tughlaq Nama, his verses follow political turns: rise of rulers, rivalries and reforms. He is poet and witness, shaping how the age remembers itself.
Later tradition links him to works like the Khaliq Bari, though scholars debate authorship. Around him, however, the real bridge stands clear: Persian of the court, Hindavi of the street.

panels.shot: somber khanqah wide shot at night

dialogue.speaker: amir_khusrau
dialogue.text: Empires pass; let my words stay beside my pir.

panels.shot: processional wide shot at Nizamuddin dargah generations later

dialogue.text: Though he died in 1325, the songs and stories around Amir Khusrau linger at Nizamuddin, carried by qawwali and memory across ages of change in Delhi.
His Indo-Persian poetry, Hindavi verse, and musical legacy helped shape north Indian culture. The bridge he built with words still stands, long after the sultans’ banners fell.
